claim: Neurotransmission is based on the exocytic fusion of synaptic vesicles (SVs) followed by endocytic membrane retrieval and the reformation of SVs.
source: Neurotransmission is based on the exocytic fusion of synaptic vesicles (SVs) followed by endocytic membrane retrieval and the reformation of SVs.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in neuroscience supported by extensive prior research, as indicated by the citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Conflicting models have been proposed regarding the mechanisms of SV endocytosis, most notably clathrin/adaptor protein complex 2 (AP-2)-mediated endocytosis and clathrin-independent ultrafast endocytosis.
source: Conflicting models have been proposed regarding the mechanisms of SV endocytosis, most notably clathrin/adaptor protein complex 2 (AP-2)-mediated endocytosis and clathrin-independent ultrafast endocytosis.
evidence: The manuscript references multiple prior studies that have proposed different mechanisms for SV endocytosis.

claim: Partitioning between clathrin-mediated and clathrin-independent endocytosis pathways has been suggested to be controlled by temperature and stimulus paradigm.
source: Partitioning between these pathways has been suggested to be controlled by temperature and stimulus paradigm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is a key context for the current study.

claim: SV endocytosis in mouse hippocampal neurons at physiological temperature occurs independent of clathrin.
source: We report on the comprehensive survey of six major SV proteins to show that SV endocytosis in mouse hippocampal neurons at physiological temperature occurs independent of clathrin
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: The endocytic retrieval of vesicular transporters for glutamate and GABA depends on sorting by the clathrin adaptor AP-2.
source: while the endocytic retrieval of a subset of SV proteins including the vesicular transporters for glutamate and GABA depend on sorting by the clathrin adaptor AP-2.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 3-8.

claim: Synaptic vesicles are tiny organelles approximately 40 nm in diameter.
source: Synaptic transmission relies on the release of neurotransmitters by calcium-triggered exocytic fusion of synaptic vesicles (SVs), tiny organelles (~40 nm in diameter)
evidence: This is established knowledge about SV structure.

claim: Synaptic vesicles store and secrete neurotransmitter molecules at specialized active zone (AZ) release sites within presynaptic nerve terminals.
source: that store and secrete neurotransmitter molecules at specialized active zone (AZ) release sites within presynaptic nerve terminals (Südhof, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Südhof, 2004.

claim: Following exocytosis, SVs are locally reformed via compensatory endocytic retrieval of membrane and its protein constituents from the cell surface to keep the presynaptic surface area constant and to ensure sustained neurotransmission.
source: Following exocytosis, SVs are locally reformed via compensatory endocytic retrieval of membrane and its protein constituents (i.e., SV proteins) from the cell surface in order to keep the presynaptic surface area constant and to ensure sustained neurotransmission (Dittman and Ryan, 2009; Kononenko and Haucke, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The core components that mediate the exo- and endocytosis of SVs have been identified and characterized in detail.
source: While the core components that mediate the exo- and endocytosis of SVs have been identified and characterized in detail (Rizzoli, 2014; Takamori et al., 2006; Wilhelm et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying SV endocytosis and reformation have remained controversial.
source: the molecular mechanisms underlying SV endocytosis and reformation have remained controversial (Delvendahl et al., 2016; Kononenko et al., 2014; Soykan et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2013; Watanabe et al., 2014; Milosevic, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies with differing conclusions.

claim: Pioneering ultrastructural analyses of stimulated frog neuromuscular junctions using electron microscopy suggested that SVs are recycled via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of plasma membrane infoldings or budding from cisternal structures located away from the AZ.
source: Pioneering ultrastructural analyses of stimulated frog neuromuscular junctions using electron microscopy (EM) suggested that SVs are recycled via clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) of plasma membrane infoldings or budding from cisternal structures located away from the AZ (Heuser and Reese, 1973).
evidence: This is a historical finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: CME occurs on a timescale of many seconds and crucially depends on clathrin and its essential adaptor protein complex 2 (AP-2).
source: Subsequent studies in neurons and in nonneuronal models showed that CME occurs on a timescale of many seconds and crucially depends on clathrin and its essential adaptor protein complex 2 (AP-2) (Mitsunari et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citation.

claim: AP-2 is a heterotetramer comprising α, β2, μ2, and σ2 subunits.
source: a heterotetramer comprising α, β2, μ2, and σ2 subunits
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about AP-2.

claim: High-pressure freezing EM paired with optogenetic stimulation has unraveled a clathrin-independent mechanism of SV endocytosis (CIE) in response to single action potential stimuli that selectively operates at physiological temperature.
source: Recent studies using high-pressure freezing EM paired with optogenetic stimulation have unraveled a clathrin-independent mechanism of SV endocytosis (CIE) in response to single action potential (AP) stimuli that selectively operates at physiological temperature (Watanabe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis (UFE) pathway is distinct from kiss-and-run or kiss-and-stay exoendocytosis observed in neuroendocrine cells.
source: This ultrafast endocytosis (UFE) pathway is distinct from kiss-and-run or kiss-and-stay exoendocytosis observed in neuroendocrine cells (Alés et al., 1999; Shin et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis operates on a timescale of hundreds of milliseconds.
source: operates on a timescale of hundreds of milliseconds
evidence: This is a characteristic of UFE from prior research.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis results in the generation of endosome-like vacuoles (ELVs) from which SVs can reform via clathrin-mediated budding processes.
source: and results in the generation of endosome-like vacuoles (ELVs) from which SVs can reform via clathrin-mediated budding processes (Kononenko et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Temperature-sensitive, clathrin-independent SV endocytosis has been observed by presynaptic capacitance recordings at cerebellar mossy fiber boutons and by optical imaging at small hippocampal synapses.
source: Temperature-sensitive, clathrin-independent SV endocytosis has also been observed by presynaptic capacitance recordings at cerebellar mossy fiber boutons and by optical imaging at small hippocampal synapses (Delvendahl et al., 2016; Kononenko et al., 2014; Soykan et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Clathrin-independent SV endocytosis is compatible with the accumulation of postendocytic presynaptic vacuoles upon acute or sustained genetic perturbation of clathrin at stimulated fly neuromuscular junctions and at mammalian central synapses.
source: and is compatible with the accumulation of postendocytic presynaptic vacuoles upon acute or sustained genetic perturbation of clathrin at stimulated fly neuromuscular junctions (Kasprowicz et al., 2014; Kasprowicz et al., 2008; Heerssen et al., 2008) and at mammalian central synapses (Kononenko et al., 2014; Imig et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work in multiple model systems.

claim: Under physiological conditions, SV endocytosis is primarily mediated by CIE (e.g., UFE), while the function of clathrin and clathrin adaptors such as AP-2 is limited to the reformation of functional SVs from internal ELVs rather than acting at the plasma membrane proper.
source: Collectively, these studies suggest that SV endocytosis under physiological conditions is primarily mediated by CIE (e.g., UFE), while the function of clathrin and clathrin adaptors such as AP-2 is limited to the reformation of functional SVs from internal ELVs rather than acting at the plasma membrane proper.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Optical imaging-based acid quench experiments in hippocampal neurons indicate that the capacity of UFE is limited to single or few APs.
source: First, optical imaging-based acid quench experiments in hippocampal neurons indicate that the capacity of UFE is limited to single or few APs
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The majority of SV proteins appear to be internalized on a timescale of several seconds following AP train stimulation.
source: while the majority of SV proteins appear to be internalized on a timescale of several seconds following AP train stimulation (Dittman and Ryan, 2009; Soykan et al., 2017; Kim and Ryan, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: High-pressure freezing EM experiments have not been able to reveal the fate and time course of endocytosis of SV proteins.
source: Second, as high-pressure freezing EM experiments have not been able to reveal the fate and time course of endocytosis of SV proteins
evidence: This is a limitation of prior experimental approaches noted by the authors.

claim: It is formally possible that UFE proceeds under conditions of clathrin depletion while SV proteins remain stranded on the neuronal surface.
source: it is formally possible that UFE proceeds under conditions of clathrin depletion (Watanabe et al., 2014), while SV proteins remain stranded on the neuronal surface.
evidence: This is a logical possibility raised by the authors based on prior findings.

claim: Mutational inactivation of the binding motifs for the clathrin adaptor AP-2 in VGLUT and VGAT severely compromises the speed and efficacy of their endocytic retrieval at room temperature.
source: Third, mutational inactivation of the binding motifs for the clathrin adaptor AP-2 in the vesicular transporters for glutamate (VGLUT) and γ-aminobutyric acid (VGAT) severely compromises the speed and efficacy of their endocytic retrieval at room temperature (Voglmaier et al., 2006; Santos et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017; Foss et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: At low temperature when UFE is blocked, VGLUT and VGAT may be retrieved from the cell surface via clathrin/AP-2.
source: arguing that at least under these conditions (e.g., low temperature when UFE is blocked) these SV proteins may be retrieved from the cell surface via clathrin/AP-2.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior experimental findings.

claim: Genetic inactivation of clathrin/AP-2-associated endocytic adaptors for the sorting of specific SV proteins causes the accumulation of their respective SV cargos at the neuronal plasma membrane.
source: Finally, genetic inactivation of clathrin/AP-2-associated endocytic adaptors for the sorting of specific SV proteins, for example Stonin 2, an adaptor for the SV calcium sensor Synaptotagmin, or AP180, an adaptor for Synaptobrevin/VAMP2, causes the accumulation of their respective SV cargos at the neuronal plasma membrane (Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Cousin, 2017; Kaempf et al., 2015; Koo et al., 2015; Mori and Takamori, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Lentiviral shRNA-mediated depletion of clathrin reduced clathrin levels to approximately 10-25% of the levels found in controls.
source: We first depleted clathrin heavy chain (CHC) in hippocampal neurons using lentiviral vectors to ~10–25% of the levels found in controls as evidenced by confocal imaging of immunostained samples and by immunoblot analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Lentiviral shRNA-mediated depletion of clathrin potently inhibited uptake of transferrin into cultured neurons.
source: Lentiviral shRNA-mediated depletion of clathrin potently inhibited uptake of transferrin into cultured neurons, indicating effective blockade of CME (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: Exo-/endocytosis of all SEP-tagged SV proteins proceeded with unaltered kinetics (τ ~ 15–20 s) irrespective of the depletion of clathrin at physiological temperature following stimulation with 200 APs at 40 Hz.
source: Strikingly, exo-/endocytosis of all SEP-tagged SV proteins proceeded with unaltered kinetics, that is τ ~ 15–20 s, irrespective of the depletion of clathrin (Figure 2C–N).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2C–N.

claim: Acute blockade of clathrin function by application of Pitstop2 did not alter the kinetics of SV protein endocytosis at physiological temperature.
source: Similar results were seen if clathrin function was acutely blocked by application of the small molecule inhibitor Pitstop2 (von Kleist et al., 2011; Figure 2O, P)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2O, P.

claim: Pitstop2 potently inhibited CME of transferrin.
source: a condition that potently inhibited CME of transferrin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Under conditions of low-frequency stimulation (200 APs at 5 Hz) at room temperature, the endocytic retrieval of Syp-SEP or VGLUT1-SEP was delayed in neurons depleted of clathrin.
source: When these experiments were repeated under conditions of low-frequency stimulation (200 APs applied at 5 Hz) at room temperature (RT), that is conditions in which the efficacy of CIE is reduced (Watanabe et al., 2014), the endocytic retrieval of Syp-SEP (also often referred to as SypHy) or VGLUT1-SEP was delayed in neurons depleted of clathrin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-J)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-J.

claim: Conditional ablation of AP-2 expression by tamoxifen induction of Cre recombinase in hippocampal neurons from Ap2m1lox/lox mice resulted in a reduction of AP-2 levels to <15% of that detected in WT control neurons.
source: We conditionally ablated AP-2 expression by tamoxifen induction of Cre recombinase in hippocampal neurons from Ap2m1lox/lox mice crossed with inducible CAG-Cre transgenic mice resulting in a reduction of AP-2 levels to <15% of that detected in WT control neurons (hereafter referred to as AP-2µ KO) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; Kononenko et al., 2014; Soykan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Endocytosis of Syt1-SEP and SV2A-SEP proceeded with similar kinetics in control or AP-2μ KO hippocampal neurons stimulated with 200 APs at 40 Hz at physiological temperature.
source: Endocytosis of Syt1-SEP and SV2A-SEP proceeded with similar kinetics in control or AP-2μ KO hippocampal neurons stimulated with 200 APs applied at 40 Hz at physiological temperature, consistent with our earlier findings (Kononenko et al., 2014; Soykan et al., 2017; Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: Loss of AP-2 significantly slowed down the endocytic retrieval of Syp, Syb2, VGLUT1, and VGAT.
source: Surprisingly, however, we found that loss of AP-2 significantly slowed down the endocytic retrieval of other major SV proteins such as Syp, Syb2, and most prominently, of the vesicular neurotransmitter transporters VGLUT1 and VGAT (Figure 3E–L).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3E–L.

claim: Plasmid-based reexpression of AP-2μ in AP-2μ KO neurons rescued defective endocytosis of SEP-tagged SV proteins.
source: These phenotypes were specific as plasmid-based reexpression of AP-2μ in AP-2μ KO neurons rescued defective endocytosis of these SEP-tagged SV proteins (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Exocytosed VGLUT1-SEP accumulates on the surface of AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: These experiments showed that exocytosed VGLUT1-SEP accumulates on the surface of AP-2μ KO neurons (Figure 3M) as quantitatively evidenced by an increased ΔF2/ΔF1 ratio (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M, N.

claim: No difference in the fraction of surface-accumulated SV2A-SEP molecules was observed in AP-2μ KO compared to WT neurons.
source: No difference in the fraction of surface-accumulated SV2A-SEP molecules was observed in AP-2μ KO compared to WT neurons (Figure 3O, P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3O, P.

claim: AP-2 is required for VGLUT1-SEP endocytosis but is dispensable for vesicle reacidification.
source: These experiments demonstrate that AP-2 is required for VGLUT1-SEP endocytosis but is dispensable for vesicle reacidification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the acid quench and folimycin experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Endocytosis of SV2A- and VGLUT1-SEP proceeded unperturbed in hippocampal neurons depleted of clathrin in response to 50 APs at 20 Hz.
source: While endocytosis of SV2A- and VGLUT1-SEP proceeded unperturbed in hippocampal neurons depleted of clathrin (Figure 4A–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: A substantial delay in the endocytosis of VGLUT1- but not SV2-SEP was observed in neurons lacking AP-2 in response to 50 APs at 20 Hz.
source: a substantial delay in the endocytosis of VGLUT1- but not SV2-SEP was observed in neurons lacking AP-2 (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E–H.

claim: No difference was found in the fraction of boutons responding to stimulation with 50 APs between WT and AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: No difference was found in the fraction of boutons responding to stimulation with 50 APs between WT and AP-2μ KO neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: At lower stimulation intensities (10 or 20 APs), AP-2μ KO neurons displayed significantly attenuated exocytic responses.
source: At lower stimulation intensities (i.e., 10 or 20 APs), AP-2μ KO neurons displayed significantly attenuated exocytic responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of AP-2 severely delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous VGAT in response to train stimulation with 200 APs at physiological temperature.
source: Loss of AP-2 severely delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous VGAT in response to train stimulation with either 200 APs (Figure 5B, C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, C using CypHer5E-labeled antibodies.

claim: Loss of AP-2 severely delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous VGAT in response to train stimulation with 50 APs at physiological temperature.
source: or 50 APs (Figure 5D, E) at physiological temperature
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, E using CypHer5E-labeled antibodies.

claim: Lentiviral shRNA-mediated depletion of clathrin had no effect on the endocytic retrieval of endogenous VGAT in response to 200 APs at 40 Hz at physiological temperature.
source: Lentiviral shRNA-mediated depletion of clathrin had no effect on the endocytic retrieval of endogenous VGAT in response to either strong (e.g., train of 200 APs applied at 40 Hz) (Figure 5F, G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F, G using CypHer5E-labeled antibodies.

claim: Lentiviral shRNA-mediated depletion of clathrin had no effect on the endocytic retrieval of endogenous VGAT in response to 50 APs at 20 Hz at physiological temperature.
source: or mild stimulation (50 APs at 20 Hz) (Figure 5H, I) at physiological temperature.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H, I using CypHer5E-labeled antibodies.

claim: Acute inhibition of clathrin function with Pitstop2 had no effect on the endocytic retrieval of endogenous VGAT at physiological temperature.
source: Similar results were obtained, if clathrin function was perturbed pharmacologically by acute inhibition in the presence of Pitstop2 in either WT or clathrin-depleted neurons (Figure 5B–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B–I.

claim: Block of clathrin function resulted in a significant reduction of the readily releasable and total recycling vesicle pool sizes.
source: However, block of clathrin function potently inhibited CME of transferrin (Figure 5J) and resulted in a significant reduction of the readily releasable and total recycling vesicle pool sizes probed by consecutive trains of 50 and 900 APs interspersed by a 90-s interstimulus interval (Gerth et al., 2017; Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J, K.

claim: The postexocytic retrieval kinetics of endogenous VGAT remained unaltered upon block of clathrin function.
source: In contrast, the postexocytic retrieval kinetics of endogenous VGAT remained unaltered (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: No difference was detected in the plasma membrane levels of Syt1 and SV2A between WT and AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: No difference was detected in the plasma membrane levels of Syt1 and SV2A between WT and AP-2μ KO neurons (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell surface biotinylation assays shown in Figure 6B–E.

claim: Significantly larger amounts of VGLUT1 and VGAT were found at the plasma membrane of AP-2μ KO neurons compared to WT controls.
source: By contrast, significantly larger amounts of VGLUT1 and VGAT were found at the plasma membrane of AP-2μ KO neurons compared to WT controls (Figure 6F–I)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell surface biotinylation assays shown in Figure 6F–I.

claim: The total levels of SV proteins assessed either by western blot or immunostaining were unaltered in AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: while the total levels of SV proteins assessed either by western blot or immunostaining were unaltered (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Application of antibodies recognizing luminal domains of VGAT and VGLUT1 under nonpermeabilizing conditions revealed elevated plasma membrane levels of VGAT and VGLUT1 in AP-2μ KO hippocampal neurons.
source: Application of these antibodies under nonpermeabilizing conditions to selectively recognize the surface-stranded SV protein pool revealed elevated plasma membrane levels of VGAT (Figure 7F–H) and VGLUT1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C) in AP-2μ KO hippocampal neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F–H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The presynaptic surface pool of Syt1 remained unaltered in AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: while the presynaptic surface pool of Syt1 remained unaltered (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B–D.

claim: Silencing of neuronal activity in the presence of TTX rescued surface stranding of VGAT in AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: Importantly, silencing of neuronal activity in the presence of the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX) rescued surface stranding of VGAT (Figure 7F–H)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F–H.

claim: Silencing of neuronal activity in the presence of TTX rescued surface stranding of VGLUT1 in AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: and VGLUT1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The observed plasma membrane accumulation of a subset of SV proteins in AP-2μ KO neurons is a consequence of defective stimulation-induced SV protein retrieval following exocytic SV fusion.
source: suggesting that the observed plasma membrane accumulation of a subset of SV proteins in AP-2μ KO neurons is a consequence of defective stimulation-induced SV protein retrieval following exocytic SV fusion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TTX rescue experiments.

claim: Robust binding of the GST-fused cytoplasmic domain of VGLUT1 to AP-2 was observed.
source: Robust binding of the GST-fused cytoplasmic domain of VGLUT1 to AP-2 was observed, whereas no association with AP-3 was detected (Figure 8B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GST pulldown assays shown in Figure 8B, C.

claim: Mutational inactivation of the putative AP-2-binding dileucine motif (F510A/V511A) in VGLUT1 largely abrogated VGLUT1 complex formation with AP-2.
source: Mutational inactivation of the putative AP-2-binding dileucine motif, that is F510A/V511A (FV/AA) (Voglmaier et al., 2006; Santos et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017), largely abrogated VGLUT1 complex formation with AP-2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GST pulldown assays shown in Figure 8B, C.

claim: A weak, possibly nonspecific interaction of VGLUT1 with AP-1 was detected that was insensitive to the FV/AA mutation.
source: We also detected a weak, possibly nonspecific interaction of VGLUT1 with AP-1 that was insensitive to the FV/AA mutation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VGLUT1 is directly recognized and binds to AP-2 via its acidic cluster dileucine motif.
source: These results show that VGLUT1 is directly recognized and binds to AP-2 via its acidic cluster dileucine motif.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GST pulldown experiments.

claim: Mutant forms of VGLUT1 or VGAT defective in AP-2 binding displayed significantly slower endocytosis kinetics compared to the respective WT proteins at physiological temperature.
source: Mutant forms of VGLUT1 or VGAT defective in AP-2 binding displayed significantly slower endocytosis kinetics compared to the respective WT proteins (Figure 8D–G, wild type in black and VGLUT1-FV/AA mutant or VGAT-F44A/AA mutant in purple).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D–G.

claim: The endocytic defects of AP-2-binding deficient mutants of VGLUT1 and VGAT were exacerbated when endocytosis was monitored at RT under conditions that might favor CME (200 APs, 5 Hz).
source: These endocytic defects were exacerbated when endocytosis was monitored at RT and under conditions that might favor CME (200 APs, 5 Hz; Kononenko et al., 2014; Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: The delayed decay of mutant VGLUT1-FV/AA-SEP signals could not be attributed to defects in reacidification.
source: Importantly, the delayed decay of mutant VGLUT1-FV/AA-SEP signals could not be attributed to defects in reacidification (e.g., caused by internalization into slowly acidifying compartments), because poststimulus application of acid solution effectively quenched its fluorescence (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Loss of AP-2 phenocopied the effect of mutational inactivation of the dileucine motifs in VGLUT1 or VGAT.
source: Strikingly, loss of AP-2 not only phenocopied the effect of mutational inactivation of the dileucine motifs in VGLUT1 or VGAT
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D–G.

claim: Combined mutational inactivation of the dileucine motifs in VGLUT1 or VGAT and AP-2μ KO did not result in additive phenotypes.
source: but combined mutational inactivation of the dileucine motifs in VGLUT1 or VGAT and AP-2μ KO did not result in additive phenotypes (Figure 8D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D–G.

claim: AP-2 directly recognizes surface-stranded VGLUT1 and VGAT via acidic cluster dileucine motifs contained in their cytoplasmic domains to facilitate their endocytic retrieval from the plasma membrane via CIE.
source: These data show that AP-2 directly recognizes surface-stranded VGLUT1 and VGAT via acidic cluster dileucine motifs contained in their cytoplasmic domains to facilitate their endocytic retrieval from the plasma membrane via CIE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: Comprehensive survey of the endocytic retrieval of six major SV proteins by optical imaging provides strong support for the notion that SV endocytosis occurs independent of clathrin at physiological temperature.
source: First, comprehensive survey of the endocytic retrieval of six major SV proteins by optical imaging conducted in two independent laboratories provides strong support for the emerging notion (Soykan et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2014) that SV endocytosis occurs independent of clathrin, corroborating the prevalence of CIE at physiological temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The endocytic retrieval of VGLUT1 and VGAT from the presynaptic plasma membrane depends on sorting by the clathrin adaptor AP-2.
source: Second and most surprisingly, we find that the endocytic retrieval of a subset of these SV proteins including VGLUT1 and VGAT from the presynaptic plasma membrane depends on sorting by the clathrin adaptor AP-2.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A fraction of endogenous VGLUT1 and VGAT molecules remain stranded on the presynaptic plasma membrane of AP-2μ KO neurons.
source: This conclusion from SEP- and CypHer5E-based imaging and acid quenching experiments of exogenously expressed or endogenous SV proteins is further corroborated by the observation that a fraction of endogenous VGLUT1 and VGAT molecules remain stranded on the presynaptic plasma membrane of AP-2μ KO neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from biotinylation and immunofluorescence assays.

claim: Surface stranding of VGLUT1 and VGAT in AP-2μ KO neurons is rescued upon silencing of neuronal activity.
source: a phenotype that is rescued upon silencing of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing TTX rescue.

claim: Impaired endocytosis of VGLUT1 in the absence of AP-2 may indirectly impact on the kinetics of Synaptophysin and Synaptobrevin/VAMP2 retrieval.
source: Impaired endocytosis of VGLUT1 in the absence of AP-2 may indirectly also impact on the kinetics of Synaptophysin and Synaptobrevin/VAMP2 retrieval (Figure 3I–L), consistent with the proposed function of VGLUT1 as a master orchestrator of the retrieval of a subset of SV proteins (Pan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and prior literature.

claim: AP-2-mediated efficient sorting of VGLUT1 and VGAT during CIE is achieved by the recognition of acidic cluster dileucine motifs by AP-2.
source: Finally, we show that AP-2-mediated efficient sorting of VGLUT1 and VGAT during CIE is achieved by the recognition of acidic cluster dileucine motifs by AP-2, in agreement with earlier biochemical and cell biological experiments (Voglmaier et al., 2006; Santos et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Defective endocytosis of VGAT and resulting defects in inhibitory neurotransmission may underlie developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused by a pathogenic loss-of-function variant of AP-2μ in human patients.
source: This mechanism may also be of pathological relevance in humans. For example, defective endocytosis of VGAT and resulting defects in inhibitory neurotransmission may underlie developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused by a pathogenic loss-of-function variant of AP-2μ in human patients (Helbig et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Dedicated endocytic adaptors such as AP-2 and others (e.g., AP180, Stonin 2) operate at the presynaptic cell surface where they recognize and recruit SV proteins to sites of CIE.
source: Our findings are most consistent with and support a mechanism of SV recycling in which dedicated endocytic adaptors such as AP-2 and others (e.g., AP180, Stonin 2) operate at the presynaptic cell surface where they recognize and recruit SV proteins to sites of CIE.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the findings.

claim: Clathrin assembly occurs downstream of CIE to reform functional SVs by budding from internal ELVs.
source: Clathrin assembly only occurs once endocytic vesicles have pinched off from the plasma membrane, that is downstream of CIE, to reform functional SVs by budding from internal ELVs.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the findings.

claim: The process of SV reformation from ELVs depends on AP-2 and other clathrin-associated endocytic proteins.
source: This process of SV reformation depends on AP-2 and other clathrin-associated endocytic proteins (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8H.

claim: AP-2 acts at two sites: endocytic sites on the presynaptic surface and on internal ELVs together with clathrin.
source: Such an integrated model, in which AP-2 acts at two sites, endocytic sites on the presynaptic surface and on internal ELVs together with clathrin
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: The proposed model explains the speed of SV endocytosis and the apparent lack of effect of clathrin loss on SV membrane internalization in various models.
source: not only explains previous observations pertaining to the speed of SV endocytosis (Delvendahl et al., 2016; Watanabe et al., 2013) and the apparent lack of effect of clathrin loss on SV membrane internalization in various models (Kononenko et al., 2014; Soykan et al., 2017; Kasprowicz et al., 2008; Heerssen et al., 2008)
evidence: This is an inference about how the proposed model reconciles prior findings.

claim: The proposed model is consistent with the slow kinetics of clathrin assembly.
source: but is also consistent with the slow kinetics of clathrin assembly (McMahon and Boucrot, 2011)
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation.

claim: The proposed model is consistent with the accumulation of SV proteins on the neuronal surface in the absence of dedicated endocytic adaptors for SV proteins.
source: and the accumulation of SV proteins on the neuronal surface in the absence of dedicated endocytic adaptors for SV proteins, for example Stonin 2, AP180/CALM (Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Cousin, 2017; Kaempf et al., 2015; Koo et al., 2015; Mori and Takamori, 2017), and AP-2 (this study).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations and the current study's data.

claim: The mechanism identified in this study also operates during UFE.
source: We speculate that the mechanism identified here also operates during UFE.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors.

claim: Recent quantitative proteomic analysis of rodent brain has revealed AP-2 but not clathrin to be highly enriched on SVs.
source: Interestingly, recent quantitative proteomic analysis of rodent brain has revealed AP-2 but not clathrin to be highly enriched on SVs (Taoufiq et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: AP-2 may interact with SV cargos prior to the bona fide endocytic process.
source: suggesting that AP-2 may interact with SV cargos prior to the bona fide endocytic process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data.

claim: Perpetual interaction of AP-2 with SV cargos might enable rapid sorting and endocytic internalization during UFE or other forms of CIE.
source: This perpetual interaction of AP-2 with SV cargos might thus enable rapid sorting and endocytic internalization, that is during UFE or other forms of CIE.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors.

claim: The findings are consistent with recent data regarding a calcium-independent form of SV endocytosis that appears to operate independent of clathrin.
source: Of note, our findings are also consistent with recent data regarding a calcium-independent form of SV endocytosis that appears to operate independent of clathrin (Orlando et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior work.

claim: Studies in mouse hippocampal neurons and in invertebrate models have identified cargo-selective roles of Stonin 2 and the related SGIP1 protein in the endocytic retrieval of Synaptotagmin 1 from the presynaptic cell surface.
source: While endocytic adaptors for SV2 have not been reported, studies in mouse hippocampal neurons (Kononenko et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2019) and in invertebrate models (Stimson et al., 2001; Phillips et al., 2010; Jung et al., 2007) have identified cargo-selective roles of Stonin 2 and the related SGIP1 protein in the endocytic retrieval of Synaptotagmin 1 from the presynaptic cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of Stonin 2 causes the partial accumulation of Synaptotagmin 1 at plasma membrane sites near the AZ, but the kinetics of SV endocytosis appeared to be even accelerated.
source: Enigmatically however, it was shown that while loss of Stonin 2 causes the partial accumulation of Synaptotagmin 1 at plasma membrane sites near the AZ, the kinetics of SV endocytosis appeared to be even accelerated (Kaempf et al., 2015; Kononenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Synaptotagmin 1 may reach sites of endocytosis either by lateral diffusion or via confinement near sites of exocytic release due to its comparably large presynaptic surface fraction.
source: One possibility therefore is that Synaptotagmin 1 due to its comparably large presynaptic surface fraction (Pan et al., 2015) does not require active endocytic sorting. Instead, it may reach sites of endocytosis either by lateral diffusion or via confinement near sites of exocytic release (Hua et al., 2011; Kononenko et al., 2013; Willig et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors supported by citations.

claim: SV2 could follow Synaptotagmin 1 via a piggy-back mechanism.
source: SV2 could follow Synaptotagmin 1 via a piggy-back mechanism (Haucke and De Camilli, 1999), consistent with the finding that both proteins can form a stable complex in vivo (Kaempf et al., 2015; Lazzell et al., 2004; Schivell et al., 1996; Yao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors supported by citations.

claim: A confinement-based mechanism may support the endocytic retrieval of other SV proteins in the absence of their specific sorting adaptors.
source: A confinement-based mechanism may also support the endocytic retrieval of other SV proteins in the absence of their specific sorting adaptors (e.g., VGLUT1 or VGAT endocytosis in AP-2µ KO neurons).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors.

claim: The findings dissent from the widely held view that AP-2 obligatorily associates with clathrin to execute its cell physiological functions, at least in CNS neurons.
source: From a more general perspective our findings dissent from the widely held view that AP-2 obligatorily associates with clathrin to execute its cell physiological functions, at least in central nervous system (CNS) neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Studies in higher fungi have uncovered a clathrin-independent role of fungal AP-2 in the polar localization of the lipid flippases DnfA and DnfB.
source: While the most well-known function of AP-2 is its involvement in CME in mammalian cells and tissues, studies in higher fungi have uncovered a clathrin-independent role of fungal AP-2 in the polar localization of the lipid flippases DnfA and DnfB (Martzoukou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: In the fungal system, AP-2 colocalizes with endocytic markers and the actin-associated protein AbpA, but not with clathrin.
source: Interestingly, in this system AP-2 is seen to colocalize with endocytic markers and the actin-associated protein AbpA, but not with clathrin (Martzoukou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: AP-2 colocalizes with a fungal homolog of Synaptobrevin in the fungal system.
source: Because AP-2 also colocalizes with a fungal homolog of Synaptobrevin (Martzoukou et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Clathrin-independent SV endocytosis at hippocampal synapses depends on actin polymerization.
source: and clathrin-independent SV endocytosis at hippocampal synapses depends on actin polymerization (Soykan et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The newly observed function of AP-2 might reflect an unexpectedly widely conserved endocytic mechanism.
source: our newly observed function of AP-2 might reflect an unexpectedly widely conserved endocytic mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on comparisons across species.

claim: Studies in AP-2 KO cells have revealed AP-2-independent forms of CME in mammals that impact on receptor sorting and signaling.
source: Conversely, studies in AP-2 KO cells have revealed AP-2-independent forms of CME in mammals that impact on receptor sorting and signaling (Pascolutti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The findings together with other studies suggest an unexpected plasticity of endocytic mechanisms in eukaryotes including the mammalian CNS.
source: Taken together our findings together with other studies suggest an unexpected plasticity of endocytic mechanisms in eukaryotes including the mammalian CNS.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion drawn from the findings and prior work.
